Akien does a great job managing the PRs. They have a decent system to enable them to review quickly and the core team does a ton of code reviews. Once you start contributing to Godot, it's pretty addicting.
For beginners Godot is not as intuitive as other engines (e.g. Unreal with it's visual blueprints). In some areas it's quite low level but generally has good documentation.
it's very easy to get started but gets more complicated and especially buggy the more of the not-widely-used features you begin to use or the larger the project becomes.

I can't agree more about how demotivating Unity is to work with... But Godot is like a breath of fresh air. Lightweight, beautiful abstractions... It crashes as much as the competitors if not more, but man is it fun!

It's still a bit janky compared to their own GDScript, but C# is supported yes. Because there are two languages though, C# is the second class citizen, you won't find as many examples on how to do things in C# as in GDScript.
It works relatively well, and actually better than in Unity (which uses an older C# version), but unfortunately it does not work everywhere. For example, it's not possible to export to the web.
Godot is a super impressive piece of kit... what they've been able to do with a relative small team puts Unity to shame.
Godot is probably one of the repos with the most open issues on GitHub (8000+ at time of writing), though it also has 34k closed issues.

It's a dream compared to UE. With openXR support built into Godot 4, within an hour I was walking around using my Index and Vive in a VR env... 90% of my effort was spent writing implementation code for my game while on UE it was spent writing integration code.

I'm in a similar boat, and eventually realized that Godot 3.5.2 is still the LTS version and still exports just great for the web... After I realized this, I decided to switch from Godot 4.0 C# to Godot 3.5.2 with GDScript and I've been happy ever since.

One thing many of the big players do that Godot doesn't is require telling the user they used that engine. If you use Unity, you need to show the Unity splash screen unless you pay the big bucks; Godot requires none of that.

There were several significant land-mines that blew up in my face and it has made me lose some confidence in the core Godot team... I think the problem is that the core team don't actually make games, they just work on an engine.
gdscript is pretty awful. It's only python-like for someone who's never used python. No list comprehensions, no tuples, no first class functions, etc.
The problem is few of those [language] bindings are mature, nor can they be expected to remain up to date. I don't know of any games in Godot using anything but GDScript or C#.
I have tried to use it something like 2 years ago and just gave up in front of the poorly documented custom scripting language they used.

I contrast, Unity to me always felt like this huge Rube Goldberg machine I have to set in motion to do anything so if you want something that starts up in seconds and has fewer dependencies I really recommend it [Godot].

I hope the quality of their pathfinding code is not indicative of the overall quality of this engine... They scan the entire open list and recompute the heuristic value for every node all so they can find the min. Yikes! Implement a binary heap.

This is actually a great proof of concept for using Godot as a cross-platform framework for desktop applications. The distribution package is incredibly simple... and vastly superior to Electron in the performance department.
Godot breathed life into my game dev hobby a few years ago, thrilled to see it getting more resources to grow.
To get some REAL traction, Godot needs some full well-known games published... we need a 'killer app' to make it really blow up.
